title: The $424 Billion Protection Gap: What Swiss Re's Index and the RiskScan 2026 Survey Say About Who Bears Disaster Losses
summary: Swiss Re puts the global natural catastrophe protection gap at $424 billion for 2025, while a survey of more than 1,700 people by Triple-I and Munich Re US finds insurers and customers see cyber, economic, weather and AI risks as connected.
description:
Two pieces of research published within days of each other in June 2026 offer a detailed look at how much of the world's disaster risk is not covered by insurance. The first is Swiss Re Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index, reported by Insurance Business on June 5. The second is RiskScan 2026, a survey released on June 8 by the Insurance Information Institute, known as Triple-I, and Munich Re US. Read together, they show a gap that is growing in dollar terms, a coverage ratio that has barely moved in a decade, and an industry that increasingly sees its risks as linked rather than separate.

Start with the headline number. Swiss Re Institute estimates that the global natural catastrophe protection gap reached $424 billion in 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024. The institute measures the gap in premium terms. It is the additional premium that would be needed to fully cover expected economic losses, beyond what is currently written. The article does not give separate totals for insured and uninsured losses, but it does report that insured losses in 2025 were $107 billion. Swiss Re says the widening of the gap is mainly the result of rising values of exposed assets, with economic growth the main driver, and that the gap has tracked nominal GDP growth. It adds that insurance cover has broadly kept pace with the growth in exposure overall. In plain terms, there are more buildings, vehicles and businesses in harm's way, worth more money, and insurance has grown with them, but not enough to close the distance.

The coverage ratio shows the same pattern. Swiss Re puts global coverage at about 27.3% in 2025, roughly flat from 2024 and up about two percentage points from 25.3% in 2015. By region, advanced EMEA rose to 41.3% from 37.1% in 2015 and advanced Asia Pacific rose to 29.1% from 22.5%. North America has been stable at roughly 40% to 42% since 2015, but uninsured losses are growing because exposure is concentrating in hazard-prone places and rebuilding costs are rising. Latin America and emerging EMEA are at about 8% to 9%, and emerging Asia at about 5%, which means almost all new exposure there is uninsured. The index offers some examples of what is possible. In Germany, fire and storm insurance covers about 99% of residential buildings, and flood cover has grown to 57% of households from about 20% two decades ago. Earthquake cover in California went the other way: only 12% of residential policies included it in 2024, against 30% at the time of the 1994 Northridge earthquake.

Looking ahead, Swiss Re says that if insured losses continue to grow at 5% to 7% a year in real terms, global insured losses could reach $186 billion by 2030, up from $107 billion in 2025. That is a projection that depends on its assumed growth rates, not a forecast of a specific year.

The second study looks at how people inside and outside the industry perceive risk. According to Insurance Business, RiskScan 2026 surveyed more than 1,700 participants in the United States and United Kingdom across five segments: consumers, small business owners, middle-market decision-makers, property and casualty agents and brokers, and property and casualty carriers. It was published in two reports, one on reinsurance exposures and one on specialty insurance. Its central finding is that respondents in every segment see cyber incidents, economic volatility, natural catastrophes, artificial intelligence, business interruption and emerging liability exposures as connected, not isolated. AI was ranked as the most impactful emerging technology across all segments. The article does not give numeric rankings. The survey also found that perils outside the traditional peak catastrophe categories, such as floods, severe storms, winter weather and wildfires, are seen as frequent and high impact, which challenges assumptions about how well catastrophe risk can be diversified. The specialty report found that cyber and flood protection gaps persist and are widening, and respondents recognised legal system abuse as a driver of rising property and casualty costs.

Several people quoted in the coverage add detail. Triple-I's chief economist, Michel Léonard, said economic conditions are amplifying insurance risk across affordability, claims severity and capital allocation. Jennifer Wilson of the broker Newfront said inconsistent policy language across insurers complicates coverage decisions. Timothy Zeilman of HSB said AI risk resembles the early days of cyber, when exposures sat largely hidden inside traditional policies, and the article cites an HSB finding that 74% of small businesses already use AI tools. Triple-I chief executive Sean Kevelighan said recognising risk is only the first step and called for collaboration to close protection gaps.

Can the gap be narrowed? Swiss Re's index includes evidence that adaptation pays. It reviewed US adaptation projects approved from 2010 to 2022, worth about $9 billion in combined nominal value. Every project with a disclosed benefit-cost ratio had positive net benefits, and the median ratio was 1.86, ranging from 1.2 for urban flood defences in Cedar Rapids to 9.63 for levees on the Middle Rio Grande. After Hurricane Sally in 2020, homes in Alabama built or retrofitted to the IBHS Fortified standard had 55% to 70% lower claim frequency, 14% to 40% lower claim severity and loss ratios 51% to 72% lower than conventional homes. Swiss Re concludes that pairing broader insurance coverage with targeted risk adaptation in exposed areas is the most viable way to narrow the gap.

What should readers take from this? For households, the practical question is whether your policy covers the perils most likely to affect you, since standard home policies often exclude flood and earthquake. For businesses, the survey's emphasis on connected risks suggests reviewing cyber, business interruption and supply-chain exposures together. For policymakers, the evidence points to a combination of prevention, building standards and risk-based planning, with insurance supporting rather than replacing them.

Two cautions apply. The protection gap is an estimate based on models and assumptions, and different institutions measure it differently, so figures from other researchers will not match. And a survey of perceptions, like RiskScan, shows what people believe, not what will happen. The two studies are best read as complementary: one measures the size of the gap, the other explains how the industry is thinking about it.
source_name: Insurance Business (citing Triple-I, Munich Re US and Swiss Re Institute)
image_alt: Insurance risk analysis and global protection gap research (illustrative)
key_points: Swiss Re Institute's index estimates the global natural catastrophe protection gap at $424 billion in 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, measured as the extra premium needed to cover expected economic losses.
Global insurance coverage was about 27.3% in 2025, roughly flat on 2024 and up about two points from 25.3% in 2015; North America has stayed between 40% and 42% since 2015.

Triple-I and Munich Re US published RiskScan 2026 on June 8, surveying more than 1,700 people in the US and UK across five market segments; respondents saw cyber, economic, catastrophe, AI and business interruption risks as connected.
Swiss Re says insured losses were $107 billion in 2025 and could reach $186 billion by 2030 if they grow 5% to 7% a year in real terms.
Swiss Re's review of US adaptation projects found a median benefit-cost ratio of 1.86, and homes built to the Fortified standard had 55% to 70% lower claim frequency after Hurricane Sally.
why_it_matters: When a disaster strikes an uninsured home or business, the loss falls on the owner, the lender or the public purse. Knowing how large the gap is, and which measures narrow it, helps households, policymakers and insurers decide where money for protection will do the most good.

title: India Opens Insurance to 100% Foreign Ownership: What the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act Changes
summary: India's amended insurance law, passed in December 2025 and in force from February 5, 2026, lets foreign investors hold up to 100% of an insurer, lowers reinsurance capital requirements and gives the regulator new powers.
description:
India has changed its insurance law to allow foreign investors to own up to 100% of an insurance company. The change came through the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, a name that translates roughly as insurance for all, protection for all. According to PRS Legislative Research, the bill was introduced and passed in the Lok Sabha on December 16, 2025, and passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 17, 2025. India Briefing reports that the regime took effect on February 5, 2026. An earlier version of this article described a May 2, 2026 notification with a specific statutory order number, which could not be confirmed against the sources reviewed, so this version relies on the dates in the legislative record and the legal commentary.

The headline change is on ownership. Foreign investors, including foreign direct investors and foreign portfolio investors, may collectively hold up to 100% of an Indian insurer's equity, subject to conditions set by the central government. India Briefing says the cap is enabled by a new Section 3AA in the Insurance Act, 1938, and that the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2025 remove the old 74% limit and align with the foreign exchange rules for non-debt instruments. The history shows steady liberalisation: a cap of 26% was raised to 49% in 2015, to 74% in 2021 and now to 100%. Governance conditions remain. The chairperson, managing director or chief executive must be an Indian citizen, which commentators describe as requiring resident Indian leadership. The sources reviewed do not describe board composition rules in detail.

The Act does more than raise the cap. It amends three laws: the Insurance Act, 1938, the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956 and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999. India Briefing says it gives the Life Insurance Corporation more operational autonomy, including the ability to open zonal offices within India and to align overseas operations with host-country regulations. PRS notes that the bill amends the LIC Act but does not set out the details on its summary page. An earlier claim that foreign ownership in LIC is capped at 20% was not confirmed in the sources reviewed for this update and is not repeated here.

Several provisions lower barriers for reinsurance and ownership changes. PRS records that the net owned fund requirement for foreign reinsurers falls from Rs 5,000 crore to Rs 1,000 crore, and the threshold at which IRDAI approval is needed for a transfer of shares rises from 1% to 5% of paid-up share capital. It also removes the Rs 100 crore minimum paid-up capital requirement for insurance co-operative societies in life, general and health insurance, extends central government powers related to special economic zones to International Financial Services Centres, and widens the definition of insurance intermediaries to include managing general agents and insurance repositories. India Briefing adds that intermediaries move to one-time licensing, that regulators may suspend a licence rather than cancel it outright, and that non-insurance entities can merge with insurers subject to regulatory approval.

The regulator receives tougher tools. According to PRS, IRDAI can approve schemes of arrangement between an insurer and a company that does not carry on insurance business. It can supersede an insurer's board of directors and appoint an administrator if the insurer is carrying on business in a manner prejudicial to policyholders. It can specify regulations on remuneration, commissions or rewards paid to agents and intermediaries, including limits, payment methods and disclosures, and it can inspect and investigate intermediaries. The Act also creates a Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund, administered by IRDAI, funded by grants and donations, penalties received by IRDAI and other sums set by regulations. This is the fund that regulations later address. The sources reviewed did not confirm the final status of those regulations.

Not everything started at once. India Briefing says Section 25, which deals with common officers and full-time officers, was excluded, and its commencement date will be announced separately.

Why does it matter? India Briefing puts the country's insurance penetration at about 3.7% of GDP, compared with a global average of about 7%. The government's goal is broader coverage, and the argument for foreign ownership is that insurers with more capital can underwrite more business and invest in distribution and technology. Skeptics point out that capital alone does not guarantee better outcomes for consumers, and that mis-selling and slow claims have been persistent complaints. Supporters of the stronger supervisory powers say they help address this by giving IRDAI clearer authority to act when a firm fails policyholders.

What should customers expect? In the short term, nothing changes for an existing policy, because the terms of a contract remain the same whoever owns the insurer. Over time, customers may see new entrants, joint ventures converted to full foreign ownership and more product choice. The checks that matter stay the same: compare premiums and benefits, read exclusions, look at the insurer's published claim settlement record and keep documents. For investors, the legislation widens the options for foreign companies, but the pace of new entry will depend on commercial decisions, not just the law.

Readers should treat the dates and provisions here as based on the legislative record and published legal analysis. For the exact legal text, the Act and the rules issued under it are the authoritative sources.
image_alt: India financial sector and insurance market liberalization (illustrative)
key_points: The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025 passed the Lok Sabha on December 16 and the Rajya Sabha on December 17, 2025, and took effect on February 5, 2026.

Foreign investment, both direct and portfolio, can collectively reach 100% of an insurer's equity under a new Section 3AA, up from 74% and earlier 49% and 26%; the chair, managing director or CEO must be an Indian citizen.
The net owned fund requirement for foreign reinsurers falls from Rs 5,000 crore to Rs 1,000 crore, and the threshold for IRDAI approval of share transfers rises from 1% to 5%.
IRDAI gains powers to supersede an insurer's board and appoint an administrator, set rules on agent commissions and inspect intermediaries; a Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund is created.
India Briefing puts insurance penetration at about 3.7% of GDP against a global average of about 7%; Section 25 on common officers was left for a separate commencement date.
why_it_matters: Insurance reaches fewer Indians than it does people in most large economies, and the government hopes more capital and competition will change that. For customers the benefits depend on whether new entrants bring better products and service, while the regulator's stronger powers are meant to protect policyholders if an insurer is badly run.

title: FCA Ends Its Premium Finance Study Without New Rules: Monthly Insurance Payments Cost Less Than in 2022, but Scrutiny Continues
summary: The Financial Conduct Authority's final report, published on February 3, found no need for an APR cap, a 0% mandate or a commission ban for monthly payment of motor and home insurance, relying instead on Consumer Duty supervision.
description:
The Financial Conduct Authority has closed its market study into insurance premium finance without introducing new rules, concluding that the cost of paying for motor and home insurance monthly has fallen and that the evidence does not justify a price cap. The regulator published its final report on February 3, 2026, according to a legal update from the law firm CMS. This article summarises that update, which does not reproduce the report itself or give absolute interest rates, so readers who need exact figures should consult the FCA's published study.

Premium finance is the arrangement under which a customer pays for insurance in monthly instalments instead of a single annual payment. In practice, the insurer or broker arranges a credit agreement, and the customer pays interest on top of the premium. CMS reports that premium finance was used in 48% of motor and home policies in 2023. That makes it one of the most common forms of consumer credit in the country, and the reason the regulator took an interest. The FCA started the market study in October 2024, according to CMS, and published its initial findings in July 2025 before the final report in February 2026.

What did the FCA find? According to CMS, average annual percentage rates on insurance premium finance fell by 4.1% on average since 2022. The summary does not say whether that is a relative fall or a fall in percentage points, and it gives no absolute APR levels. It also reports that broker interest rates were around 3%, higher than those of insurers and intermediary lenders, which suggests that where a customer arranges finance can affect the price. The regulator found no evidence that credit risk was being double counted, meaning that customers were being charged for the risk of non-payment both in the insurance premium and again in the interest. It found that price comparison websites provide transparency by showing premium finance within the total cost of insurance. It found some brokers' exclusivity arrangements did not cause harm, though firms should ensure they meet fair value requirements under the Consumer Duty. It found no evidence of egregious commissions or high margins among brokers. It also decided that standard broker remuneration did not amount to the discretionary commission arrangements that caused concern in motor finance, so an intervention modelled on that case was not considered necessary.

Equally important is what the FCA decided not to do. It imposed no sector-wide intervention and made no rule changes. In July 2025 it had provisionally considered several options, including a cap on APRs, a mandated 0% APR and a ban on commission. In the final report it did not adopt any of them, finding that a single market-wide intervention was not proportionate. On the idea of requiring 0% finance, CMS reports the FCA said this could restrict access for customers who need the flexibility of monthly payment and could increase premiums for all policyholders. The reasoning is that if insurers could not earn anything on finance, the cost might be spread into higher annual prices that everyone pays, including customers who pay in full.

The regulator did not walk away. According to CMS, it will continue to focus on fair value through the Consumer Duty, which came into force in 2023, with stronger supervisory action against individual firms where needed. It will continue to monitor prices and use its wider regulatory tools to address competition problems or poor practices. The legal update links these steps to wider discussion of reforming the Consumer Credit Act 1974. In other words, the issue is closed as a market study but remains on the supervisory agenda.

The reaction has not been uniform. The law firm's headline describes the outcome as a clean bill of health, reflecting a view that the market is working well enough. The consumer group Which? published an article whose headline, as shown in search results, criticises the FCA for failing to act on premium finance, though this review has not read it in full. That contrast reflects a real debate about whether a market that has become cheaper but still charges interest on a necessary product is fair.

What should customers do? First, compare the total cost of paying monthly against paying annually. Every quote should show the annual premium and the total amount payable in instalments, and the difference is the cost of credit. Second, check the APR, not just the monthly amount, because a low monthly payment can hide a high interest rate. Third, consider where you arrange finance. If paying annually is possible, even by using a credit card with a lower rate or a savings pot, it may cost less, though credit card use brings its own risks. Fourth, look at what happens if you cancel mid-year, because outstanding instalments and fees can apply. Fifth, use comparison sites that show premium finance in the total cost, which the FCA found improves transparency.

For insurers and brokers, the message is that the Consumer Duty is the main tool. Firms need to be able to show that the price customers pay for finance is fair value, particularly where they receive commission or have exclusive arrangements. The regulator has said it will act against individual firms, and the decision not to cap prices does not protect those with outlying rates.

The next stage depends on the data the FCA gathers. If average prices rise again or particular firms stand out, it could return to the options it set aside. For now, the decision leaves customers with a market that is cheaper than in 2022 on average, with no price cap, and with the responsibility to compare.
source_name: CMS (summary of the FCA final report)
image_alt: UK Financial Conduct Authority building and regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA published its final report on insurance premium finance on February 3, 2026, after launching the market study in October 2024 and publishing initial findings in July 2025.
Premium finance was used in 48% of motor and home insurance policies in 2023, and average APRs have fallen 4.1% since 2022, according to the summary.
The FCA found no evidence that credit risk is double counted in both premiums and interest charges, and no evidence of egregious commissions or high margins among brokers.
It did not adopt the options it considered in July 2025, an APR cap, a mandated 0% APR or a commission ban, finding a single market-wide intervention was not proportionate.
The regulator will keep monitoring prices and use the Consumer Duty and its wider tools against individual firms where fair value is not met.
why_it_matters: Millions of UK households pay for car and home insurance monthly, and the interest on that arrangement is easy to overlook. The FCA's decision means no new price controls for now, so comparing the total cost of paying monthly with paying annually remains the customer's best protection.

title: US Car Insurance Costs Edge Up in 2026: Insurify's Mid-Year Report Shows Rises in 27 States After a 6% Fall in 2025
summary: Insurify puts the average full-coverage premium at $2,237 a year at mid-2026, up 1% since the end of 2025, with Connecticut up 10% and 32 states expected to see year-over-year increases by December.
description:
American car insurance prices have started to rise again after a year of declines, according to Insurify's mid-year report for 2026, though the national increase so far is small and the picture differs sharply from state to state. The figures were reported by Repairer Driven News and CollisionWeek on August 11, 2026. Insurify is an online insurance comparison company, and its numbers are based on the quotes it collects, so they describe the market it observes and not every policy in force. An earlier version of this article cited projections from a second company that could not be verified, so this version relies only on the Insurify report as described in the two trade publications.

Start with the national picture. Insurify says the average annual cost of full-coverage car insurance was $2,237 at mid-year, up 1% since the end of 2025. It projects that the average will reach $2,242 by the end of 2026, an increase of 1% over the year. That follows a 6% decrease in 2025, when insurers lowered rates and the average driver paid $140 less by year-end than twelve months earlier, according to Repairer Driven News. Insurify describes the change as a seven percentage point swing in the national trend. The earlier Insurify estimates reported in February used a different baseline, so figures should only be compared within the same report.

The number of states where prices are rising is the more telling change. In the first half of 2026, rates rose in 27 states, compared with nine states in the second half of 2025. Insurify projects increases in 32 states by the end of the year, with the largest expected in Connecticut at about 4% and West Virginia at about 3%. CollisionWeek notes that the steepest projected increase is in Connecticut, and that repair-cost inflation sits near the center of the reversal.

The largest first-half moves were in Connecticut, where the average rose 10%, or about $251 a year, the largest increase nationally. Kentucky rose 6%, West Virginia 5% and Illinois 4%. At the other end, Washington, D.C., New York and New Jersey each fell by at least 5%, and New Mexico, Massachusetts, Florida, Arkansas, South Dakota, Nebraska and Oklahoma saw decreases of between 2% and 5%. For the rest of the year, Insurify projects decreases of 1% to 3% in New Mexico, Arkansas, Minnesota, Colorado, Idaho, Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Iowa and New Hampshire. The Repairer Driven News article also says residents in 39 states saw relief from rising premiums, but that figure overlaps with the 27 states reported above and may refer to a different measure, so it is not relied on here.

How expensive is it? Seven states and Washington, D.C. average more than $3,000 a year for full coverage. The five most expensive places named are Washington, D.C. at $3,880, Maryland at $3,646, Rhode Island at $3,611, Michigan at $3,229 and Georgia at $3,109. Those figures are averages for a standard driver profile in Insurify's data. Individual premiums depend on age, driving record, vehicle, location and coverage, and can be far higher or lower.

What is driving prices up? Insurify points to the cost of claims and repairs. According to the report, bodily injury claims rose 36% nationally from 2020 to 2024 and collision claims rose 42%, and the report links dense Northeast urban areas with more accidents and costlier claims. Auto maintenance and repair costs rose 45% over five years, roughly double the rate of general inflation. It also cites higher fuel prices, with gasoline rising from about $3 to about $4 a gallon, and says inflation hit a three-year high in May while consumer sentiment reached a record low. The coverage reviewed does not mention tariffs or vehicle theft as drivers, so this article does not attribute the increase to either. Other analysts have pointed to those factors in the past, but they are not part of this report as described.

Insurify's figures show a reversal: rates fell in 2025 and are now rising again in most states, with repair and claims costs cited as the main pressure. A rise of 1% nationally masks big differences, so a driver in Connecticut faces a very different market from one in New Mexico.

What can drivers do? Shop around at renewal, because rates vary widely between insurers for the same driver, and the insurer that was cheapest last year may not be now. Ask about discounts for bundling policies, safe-driving programs, low mileage and anti-theft devices. Review your coverage levels and deductibles, remembering that raising the deductible reduces the premium but increases what you pay after a claim. Keep a clean driving record and check your credit-based insurance score where it is permitted. Finally, avoid letting coverage lapse, since a gap can raise prices later and leave you exposed.

The year-end figure will show whether Insurify's projection of 32 states was accurate. If repair costs and claims keep rising, increases may spread. If competition and lower claims return, prices could stabilise. For now, the data suggest a slow upturn rather than a repeat of the sharp rises of 2022 to 2024.
source_name: Repairer Driven News (citing Insurify's 2026 Mid-Year Auto Insurance Report)
image_alt: Car insurance and US auto insurance premium increase 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Insurify's mid-year report puts the national average for full coverage at $2,237 a year, up 1% since the end of 2025, and projects $2,242 by year-end, following a 6% fall in 2025.
Rates rose in 27 states in the first half of 2026, compared with nine states in the second half of 2025, and Insurify projects increases in 32 states by year-end.

Connecticut had the largest first-half rise at 10%, about $251 more a year, followed by Kentucky at 6%, West Virginia at 5% and Illinois at 4%; Washington, D.C., New York and New Jersey each fell at least 5%.
The most expensive places for full coverage were Washington, D.C. at $3,880, Maryland at $3,646, Rhode Island at $3,611, Michigan at $3,229 and Georgia at $3,109.
Insurify cites repair and maintenance costs up 45% over five years, bodily injury claims up 36% and collision claims up 42% from 2020 to 2024, and higher fuel prices as cost pressures.
why_it_matters: After a year of falling prices, drivers in many states are seeing premiums rise again. Understanding what pushes prices up, and that changes vary widely by state, helps drivers decide when shopping around is worth the effort.

title: BaFin's Third Cyber Insurance Survey: German Premiums Reach About €807 Million as Accumulation Risk Remains the Main Worry
summary: The German regulator's survey of 179 primary insurers shows stand-alone cyber premiums growing about 13% in 2024 to roughly €807 million, with small and medium-sized firms a rising share and most insurers still not pricing accumulation risk.
description:
Germany's financial regulator has published the most detailed public picture yet of the country's cyber insurance market, and it shows a business that is still growing but at a much slower pace than before. The Federal Financial Supervisory Authority, known as BaFin, published its third survey of the cyber insurance market on May 29, 2026. Its figures come from insurers' own returns and describe the market up to the end of 2024. The article on BaFin's website is the source for every number below, although some details may appear only in charts that the text does not reproduce.

The survey covered 179 primary insurers, 28 reinsurers and 14 branches, up from 178, 10 and 12 in the 2023 survey. Among them, 66 provide direct stand-alone cyber business, up from 64 in 2023 excluding branches, and 25 provide inward reinsurance, up from 22. BaFin used profit and loss data for 2022 to 2024 under German commercial accounting rules, and updated the figures for 2020 and 2021 for comparison. An important regulatory change sits behind the data. Cyber is now treated as a separate insurance class. Separate reporting under the German Insurance Reporting Regulation applies from financial year 2025, and an EU-level reporting obligation has applied since financial year 2023. That means future surveys should be more complete.

On premiums, BaFin reports that direct stand-alone gross written premiums were about €807 million in 2024. Including branches and cyber add-on cover, the figure was about €932 million. Direct premiums grew about 13% in 2024, compared with about 10% in 2023, but that is far below the growth of about 66% in 2021 and 56% in 2022. The market is therefore still expanding, though the explosive phase seems to have ended. Inward reinsurance, where primary insurers pass risk to reinsurers, tells a different story. Stand-alone inward reinsurance premiums were about €1,635 million in 2024. Growth was about 2% in 2023 and then premiums fell about 26% in 2024, after growth of roughly 54% in 2021 and 72% in 2022. BaFin cites market saturation and lower prices resulting from greater reinsurance capacity as the causes.

The customer mix is changing. Small and medium-sized enterprises accounted for about 25% of gross written premiums in 2024, up from about 15% in 2020, while large corporates fell from about 85% to about 75%. BaFin notes that the move towards smaller firms was stronger in Germany. Private customers account for less than 1% of premiums, so cyber insurance remains a business product. The international share of direct premiums fell from 54% in 2020 to 48% in 2024, meaning German insurers are writing a larger share at home.

Profitability is a major theme. BaFin reports that the gross combined ratio in direct business was below 100% in every year except 2021. A combined ratio below 100% means the insurer's claims and costs were lower than its premiums. The net combined ratio, after reinsurance, was above 100% in every year except 2020, which BaFin says shows strong reliance on reinsurance. For inward reinsurance, the net combined ratio was below 100% only in 2020 and 2023. International business shows wider swings in combined ratios than German business, and inward reinsurance retention fell slightly in 2024. In simple terms, direct insurers have been able to price at a profit before reinsurance, but they lean heavily on reinsurers to keep the book balanced.

The regulator's main concern is accumulation. This describes a situation where one event, such as an attack on a widely used software supplier or a cloud service, causes claims across many policyholders at the same time. BaFin says accumulation losses have been observed more often in large corporates and, within that segment, increasingly in international business. It reports that most insurers analyse accumulation losses in direct business but just under half factor them into premiums. It also notes that insurers lack comprehensive cyber claims data and that loss scenarios can change quickly. That combination, limited history and fast-changing threats, makes pricing and reserving difficult. Cyber claims are usually settled within three years, though cases involving SMEs and especially large corporates take longer.

What does this mean for businesses? Companies that buy cyber cover should expect insurers to ask detailed questions about security controls, because insurers are trying to understand their accumulation exposure. They should read the policy wording closely for exclusions related to widespread events or infrastructure failures, and check what limits apply. For SMEs, which are an increasing share of the market, the survey suggests insurers want this business, but the long-term pricing is not settled. Businesses should not assume that premiums will stay at today's levels.

For insurers, the survey suggests two lessons. The first is that reliance on reinsurance has been high, and the recent fall in reinsurance premiums reflects cheaper reinsurance capacity, which may not last. The second is that building models for accumulation and including them in prices is still a work in progress for around half the market.

BaFin's analysis does not forecast losses or recommend products. It describes what insurers reported, and some details, such as the number of policies with ransom cover, are collected but not stated in the text. Readers should therefore treat the figures as a snapshot of 2024 rather than the current state of the market. An earlier version of this article cited a Munich Re estimate that the global cyber insurance market at about $15 billion of premiums in 2025, could not be confirmed in this review and is not relied on here. The next survey, and the separate reporting that began for financial year 2025, will show whether growth recovers and whether insurers narrow the pricing gap on accumulation.
image_alt: Cybersecurity and cyber insurance risk management in Germany (illustrative)
key_points: BaFin published its third cyber insurance market survey on May 29, 2026, covering 179 primary insurers, 28 reinsurers and 14 branches, with profit and loss data for 2022 to 2024.
Direct stand-alone cyber premiums were about €807 million in 2024, or about €932 million including branches and cyber add-on cover, growing about 13% after about 10% in 2023.
Stand-alone inward reinsurance premiums were about €1,635 million in 2024, a fall of about 26%, which BaFin links to market saturation and lower prices from greater reinsurance capacity.
Small and medium-sized enterprises' share of premiums rose from about 15% in 2020 to about 25% in 2024; private customers account for under 1%.
Most insurers analyse accumulation losses in direct business but just under half factor them into premiums, and insurers lack comprehensive claims data.
why_it_matters: Cyber insurance is meant to help businesses recover from attacks, but a single event that hits many customers at once could strain insurers. BaFin's figures show a market that is growing more slowly, shifting towards smaller firms and still learning how to price its biggest risk.

title: MAS Sets Rules for Digital Advertising and 'Finfluencers': Five Safeguards for Firms and Warning Letters to Five Content Creators
summary: Singapore's central bank issued guidelines, effective March 25, 2026, on how financial institutions and the creators they hire must advertise products online, and said it would write to five creators who may have given financial advice without a licence.
description:
Singapore has set out how banks, insurers and other financial firms must behave when they promote products on social media, and it has put creators who give financial advice online on notice. The Monetary Authority of Singapore announced a package of measures that included guidelines on digital advertising and a guide for content creators, according to a summary by the law firm Linklaters whose article is dated October 1, 2025. The guidelines take effect on March 25, 2026, so they are now in force. This article summarises the Linklaters account, which describes the MAS announcements and does not reproduce the underlying documents, so details should be checked against MAS publications.

The main document is the Guidelines on Standards of Conduct for Digital Advertising Activities. They apply to all financial institutions regulated by MAS and to third parties that those institutions appoint to advertise financial products and services to customers through digital media. That second group matters, because it is what brings so-called finfluencers into the framework. A finfluencer is a content creator who talks about, reviews or promotes financial products to an online audience. If a bank or insurer pays or otherwise engages such a person to promote a product, the guidelines hold the institution responsible for what is said.

According to Linklaters, there are five main requirements. First, the institution must assess whether the choice of digital media is appropriate for the product, which requires new processes to judge appropriateness. A complex or high-risk product may not suit a short video or a post with limited space. Second, the firm must assess the characteristics and limitations of the medium and present important disclosures prominently and clearly. MAS gives an extensive list of example disclosures. Third, the firm must assess and select its digital marketers and ensure they are told about, and comply with, the institution's digital advertising practices and the regulatory requirements. Fourth, the firm must monitor the digital marketers' advertising activities. Fifth, it must take appropriate disciplinary action against digital marketers to deter malpractice. MAS will hold the board and senior management accountable for compliance with the guidelines, which signals that the issue is expected to be dealt with at the top of the organisation and not left to the marketing team.

The second document is aimed at creators. Linklaters describes a Guide on Responsible Financial Content Creation, developed by MAS together with a body it abbreviates as ASAS. It sets out seven things creators must know when sharing financial information online, including when an MAS licence may be required and the need to disclose any compensation they receive. The practical effect is to give creators a checklist for staying on the right side of the rules, and to remind them that being paid to promote a product is something their audience is entitled to know.

The most direct action concerns five individuals. According to the article, MAS said it would issue advisory letters to five content creators who may have provided financial advice without a licence. Those creators were advised to adjust their content and practices to meet MAS requirements. The article says that persons who continue to provide financial advice without a licence will face enforcement action. It does not name the creators, describe the content involved or specify the penalties that could apply under the guidelines. The use of advisory letters, rather than prosecution, shows a first step designed to correct behaviour before escalating.

Why is the regulator doing this now? Social media has become a major channel for financial information, particularly for younger investors. The risks are familiar. A creator may promote a product without explaining the risks, may be paid by the provider without saying so, or may recommend something unsuitable for the audience. Because the content is short, shareable and personal, it can be more persuasive than a formal brochure. By placing duties on the firm and the creator, MAS aims to ensure that the same standards of fairness and clarity apply to a video as to a printed advertisement. The article does not report any consultation on the guidelines, and it does not give the scale of the problem.

What does it mean in practice? For financial institutions, the guidelines mean that influencer marketing needs contracts, briefing, monitoring and the ability to take action, and that senior managers cannot say they were unaware. For creators, the key questions are whether they are giving advice, which may require a licence, and whether they are disclosing paid relationships. A creator who only discusses general information may be on safer ground than one who recommends specific products to individuals, although the dividing line is a legal question. For audiences, the changes should mean clearer disclosures, but they do not remove the need to check claims. Any promotion of an investment or insurance product should be checked against the firm's own documents and the register of licensed entities on the MAS website.

It is also worth noting what the sources do not say. The Linklaters article does not report how many firms have changed their practices since March 25, and it does not describe any enforcement action taken under the guidelines so far. Earlier coverage of this topic mentioned other Singapore regulatory initiatives in 2026, but those are outside the scope of the verified summary used here and are not repeated.

The next developments to watch are whether MAS publishes details of enforcement, whether other regulators in the region adopt similar approaches, and how firms adjust their agreements with creators. The guidelines now apply, and the question is how strictly they will be enforced.

key_points: MAS announced its Guidelines on Standards of Conduct for Digital Advertising Activities around October 1, 2025, with effect from March 25, 2026.
The guidelines apply to all financial institutions and the third parties they appoint, including finfluencers, to advertise financial products and services through digital media.

Firms must assess whether digital media suits the product, present disclosures prominently, select and brief digital marketers, monitor their advertising and take disciplinary action against malpractice.
MAS says it will hold boards and senior management accountable for compliance.
MAS said it would issue advisory letters to five content creators who may have given financial advice without a licence, and that those who continue face enforcement action.
why_it_matters: Many people now learn about investments and insurance from social media. The rules put responsibility on the firms that pay creators to promote products and warn creators that advice without a licence can bring enforcement, which affects what consumers see and how much they can trust it.
